subsystems.name: Immutable boot ROM
subsystems.role: the first code that runs; it verifies the next stage before handing over control.
parts: hash of the trusted public key

subsystems.name: Key store
subsystems.role: holds device-unique private keys and secrets that never leave the chip.

subsystems.name: Cryptographic engine
subsystems.role: performs encryption, signing, hashing and random-number generation.

subsystems.name: Secure processor or state machine
subsystems.role: runs the trusted functions in isolation from the main CPU.

subsystems.name: Tamper detection and response
subsystems.role: senses physical attacks and wipes secrets if the chip is opened or probed.

subsystems.name: Host interface
subsystems.role: lets the main system talk to the root of trust.

buildSteps.title: Define the threat model
buildSteps.detail: Decide which attacks the chip must resist — firmware tampering, key extraction, rollback — and write the security requirements.

buildSteps.title: Design the digital logic
buildSteps.detail: Engineers write the register-transfer level code for the cryptographic engines, boot ROM and secure state machine.

buildSteps.title: Verify formally and by simulation
buildSteps.detail: Mathematical proofs and millions of simulated cycles check that the boot sequence and crypto operations cannot be bypassed.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the silicon
buildSteps.detail: The design is taped out to a CMOS foundry, where transistors and metal layers are built on a silicon wafer.

buildSteps.title: Provision secrets
buildSteps.detail: In a secure facility, unique keys and certificates are generated and written into one-time-programmable fuses; the chips are then locked.

buildSteps.title: Package with anti-tamper features
buildSteps.detail: The die is covered by a shield mesh and sensors, then sealed so that opening the package erases the keys.

buildSteps.title: Certify
buildSteps.detail: Independent labs test the chip against standards such as FIPS 140 or Common Criteria before it can be sold for secure use.

buildSteps.title: Integrate into the system
buildSteps.detail: Firmware and operating-system boot code are written to ask the root of trust to verify each stage and to sign device identities.

prerequisites.why: the root of trust must be a physical chip that is hard to clone or modify.
AES, SHA and elliptic-curve cryptography are the building blocks the chip implements.

prerequisites.tech: Secure key provisioning and supply chain
prerequisites.why: unique keys must be injected without being copied or stolen during manufacturing.
physical access to the chip must not reveal its secrets.
strong keys require unpredictable numbers from a physical source, not software.
future quantum computers could break today's public-key algorithms, so new ones must be built into hardware.

pathway.unlocks: long-lived devices that stay secure against future quantum attacks.
